messages.author: c9d3aa9c565539f5
messages.subject: Stratification?
parts:
This problem, we have been struggling for the last few days, without much success. Kindly help.

Let us take an example of species X in the study site.
Let the site be divided into three strata, viz. Open Forest, Moderate Forest and Dense Forest.

We have total of nine transects, three eventually laid in each stratum.

Our idea is to obtain results with minimum CV (say about 10-20) and project results for long term monitoring. Logistics and changing encounter rate, visibility and weather are important constraints in increasing the number of spatial replicates.

Now we know that the species X is rarely found in Open Forest stratum, and populates the Dense Forest stratum well. What shall be our approach in order to obtain reliable results. We know that stratum Open Forest has very little of species X, but have to sample that area for this species for the sake of extrapolating results to the whole study site.

I made a querry regarding the same issue a few days ago and found replies promptly regarding keeping the number of samples to 9 instead of 1 (all lengths pooled). But what happens to the results in case of heterogenous habitats of a study site. Is there a method to reduce that CV which probably inflates due to the samples laid in "Open Forest" stratum (no or very less distribution of target species). What shall we do to further make our study design more efficient ?

I tried post stratifying the analysis and found the following CVs of the three different strata:
1. Dense Forest: CV = 16.53 % ; # observations = 99
2. Moderate Forest: CV = 47.08 % ; # observations = 107
3. Open Forest: CV = 139.48 % ; # observations = 6

Do these CVs have something to do with possible improper stratification? Will restratification by dividing lines into different strata help in some cases where a particular transect line runs through various strata? What shall be the number of samples in this case. Our 9 transects (spatial replicates) were walked 12 times each (temporal replicates). If I am not mistaken, variance for estimation of CVs is calculated with help of encounter rates on individual sample (line) and overall encounter rates.

Looking forward to some help.


Koustubh Sharma
INDIA.

messages.author: d718c6bb1db28db2
messages.subject: Re: Stratification?
parts:
Koustubh, your high cv's have nothing to do with improper stratification,
the problem is the lack of spatial replication - coupled with the small
number of detections in one stratum. If you can't have more, shorter
lines, then I would not stratify - I would put your 9 lines randomly
distributed throughout the study area (or more likely,
systematically-spaced lines, with the grid of lines randomly located).
The heterogeneity in density does not invalidate your abundance estimate.
You are right that in principle, stratification should improve your
precision, but you simply don't have sufficient replication in space to
stratify. Even without any stratification, you don't really have
sufficient replication in space, with just 9 lines.

Different detectability in your different strata won't bias
your estimate of abundance for the entire study area, due to the pooling
robustness property of line transect estimators, though if you calculate
separate estimates for each forest type, having used pooled data to
estimate the detection function, these are likely to be
biased. (e.g. animals are likely to be more detectable in open forest, so
you will underestimate effective strip width in this stratum by pooling
data, and hence overestimate abundance in this stratum.)

Steve

messages.author: 4b4a7b00c1dd09c7
messages.subject: Re: Stratification?
parts:
Hi Koustubh, List,

3 lines per stratum is far too few for reliable estimation of variation in
encounter rate. Indeed 9 lines is rather too few even ignoring the
stratification. I think you should focus your survey effort on getting more
(possibly shorter) lines. You will probably also have to reduce the temporal
replication to achieve this.

Section 7.2.1 of Introduction to Distance Sampling discusses transect layout,
and warns against the dangers of overstratification. It may seem intuitive to
stratify effort so that you put more effort per unit area into high density
strata (see section 7.2.2.3), but if you end up with some strata with very few
lines in them you loose reliability. Since you are going to struggle to have
enough lines per stratum for reliable estimation of encounter rate, and you are
also going to struggle to have enough observations in your low density stratum
to estimate detection function separately for that stratum, I suggest you use
the same allocation of effort per unit area for all 3 strata (in other words
same number of lines per unit area). That way you can combine the strata
together at the analysis stage if required, since coverage probability on all 3
is the same (see section 7.2.1). This assumes you are mostly interested in
estimating abundance in the forest as a whole. Alternatively you could ignore
stratification altogether and allocate lines systematically throughout the study
area (rather than systematically within strata).

If you could potentially have far more lines per stratum then look at the
allocation formulae of section 7.2.2.3.

If you want to do stratified anlyses, but don't really have a good number of
lines per stratum (but do have more than 3!), you could consider estimating
spatial variation in encounter rate by estimating an overdispersion factor
common to all strata -- see formula 3.127 and text around that, and section
8.4.1 for a detailed example.

With your current data, given the small number of lines I think you should
regard the inferences you get as preliminary. If your 3 strata are equal areas
then you have the same effort per stratum so you could try pooling strata to get
more reliable inference (although the CV will be high due to high variation in
encounter rate between lines). Alternatively, you could try the overdispersion
method mentioned above. Since you have so few detections in the low density
stratum you will have to estimate detection function pooled over strata -- this
will cause some bias if coverage probability is not even across strata.

Hope this helps,

- Len
